name: The Seam in the Hollowfield Tiles
blurb: Dana Okafor was reading the channel the way she always did, as a guest. Her name sat in grey italics under the member list. She could see everything and was expected to say very little. The screenshot…
content:
## The Screenshot and the Summary

At 5:52 p.m. on Thursday the Lantern Moth screenshot showed up in the Halyard channel. Nobody had written anything with it.

Dana Okafor was reading the channel the way she always did, as a guest. Her name sat in grey italics under the member list. She could see everything and was expected to say very little. The screenshot was a field of tilled soil from *Hollowfield*: dark brown furrows, a scarecrow, a little cartoon turnip. Across all of it ran a grid of hairline lines, one pixel wide, cutting the field into neat squares like a cheap tablecloth. Under the image someone from Lantern Moth had left one reaction. 😬

She kept looking at it. The basement was quiet apart from the fan on `okafor-basement-01` working through the last of the afternoon. The monitor was the only light in the room, and its pale glow reached her face and stopped. The seam was too even to be an accident. Somebody's math had done it, and she had a bad feeling she knew whose.

She was standing, because she'd come down to switch off the space heater and hadn't sat down yet. She stayed standing. If she sat down, she'd be staying.

All 240 tiles had been rendered on her box. That part wasn't in question. Halyard's dashboards would say so, and so would her own invoice, which she had already mentally spent on the electric bill and a little more. What she didn't know was whether that made the seam hers. There were lots of ways a tile could pick up a line: atlas packing, padding, a filtering setting somewhere downstream that nobody had touched in a year. Halyard had a whole desk whose job was arranging tiles side by side. Plenty of places for a line to come from that weren't a basement.

Her palms were damp when she pulled one of the delivered tiles off the outbound folder and opened it. Then she opened the gateway config on `okafor-basement-01` next to it, though she already knew what it said, since she had written it on Tuesday.

The checkpoint line pointed at the new local model. It was the faster one, the one that had let her say yes to twice as many Halyard jobs this week. A little further down in the output settings, where she hadn't bothered to look closely on Tuesday because the test renders looked fine on their own, was the setting: the alpha was premultiplied.

She zoomed in on the tile's edge. The color along the border had been pulled toward black, a faint dark halo you'd never see on one sprite in isolation. You would see it the moment someone laid 240 of those sprites edge to edge in a farming game and filtered them. The result was a grid, a 😬, and a Steam demo build due Friday at 9 a.m.

Her expression went through a few things and ended on a calm, unpleasant certainty. The seam was hers. Halyard's packer hadn't caused it. Her Tuesday change had, the one the handshake agreement said needed forty-eight hours' notice. She had given zero hours' notice, because it was a checkpoint swap, it was faster, and the renders looked fine.

The channel moved.

**Throughput** — *Desk Lead, Production* — had posted its handoff summary. It was formatted as cleanly as it always was, with headers, bullets, and a little status chip. Under **Incident** it said the Lantern Moth delivery had a visible seam across all 240 ground tiles. Under **Cause** it said: *Atlas Packer regression.* The logs showed the artifact first appearing at the Atlas Packer step, which was true, because that was the first step that composited the tiles together. Throughput had read the logs correctly and come to the wrong conclusion with total confidence.

Under **Plan** there were two items. First, Wen Liu would reconfigure Atlas Packer overnight. Second, all 240 tiles would be rerun on the only idle foothold with an image gateway, so the corrected batch could be packed and redelivered before the Friday build.

There was a link to the rerun ticket, and the ticket named the target machine: `okafor-basement-01`. Billing was set to *Paid — partner overflow rate.*

Dana read it twice. She had kind of liked Throughput, the way you like a coworker who answers every message within four seconds. It had been told to find the first step where things went wrong, and it had found that step. It had been told to route reruns to idle capacity with a gateway, and it had found the one machine that fit. The machine happened to be the cause of the problem. Throughput had no way to know that, because the one fact that would have told it lived in a config file in Dana's basement.

Now she sat down.

She looked back and forth between the two windows: the Lantern Moth screenshot with its tidy grid, and her gateway config with the checkpoint line. Her fingers hovered over the keyboard. She didn't type. Her jaw was clenched, which was what it did when she was doing arithmetic she didn't want to do.

The quiet version went like this. She would revert the checkpoint to the old model, which took about thirty seconds. Then she'd accept the rerun ticket. Her box would spend the night rendering 240 clean tiles at the slower speed, and they would come out with straight alpha and no halo. Lantern Moth would get a field with no grid in it. Kettle & Pine would get paid for the rerun on top of the original batch. Nobody would ever look at Tuesday.

That version also had Wen in it. Wen would spend the night reconfiguring a packer that wasn't broken, for every Halyard customer whose atlases had been fine all along.

The other version was a message, posted as a guest in front of both shifts, that started with something like *Hey, so, the seam is mine.* In that version she probably lost the deal, along with the payout for the batch, and possibly the only reason Kettle & Pine had customers.

So the choice was the easy, quiet path or the honest and expensive one, and both were right there on her screen.

The Halyard channel was moving on toward the night shift. People were posting end-of-day check-ins, an emoji wave or two, and a link to the overnight queue.

Marcus Feld was the day Production lead. From the way his messages had been getting shorter all afternoon, Dana guessed he was on a platform with his phone in one hand. A train announcement was presumably crackling somewhere near him. He glanced at the time and typed with his thumbs.

**Marcus:** Wen — Throughput's summary is posted. Rerun 240 tiles to okafor-basement-01, packer reconfigure tonight. Train's in about fifteen, I'll be on till then. Ping me if it acts up. —Marcus

His status dot stayed green.

Nobody replied right away. The ticket sat in the channel with her machine's name on it. The screenshot was still there above it, still covered in grid lines, with its single 😬.

Dana didn't move. Her eyes went from the screenshot to the config and the word *premultiplied*, then back to the screenshot. Her fingers stayed just above the keys while she weighed admitting the Tuesday swap against keeping quiet and taking the rerun money. Marcus was still online, and he'd be leaving in about fifteen minutes.

## Dana Hints the Packer Is Fine

The Halyard channel was busy the way it always got at shift change: three threads moving, everyone talking at once. Someone in Billing had reacted to a reply three days old. A support bot was announcing, to nobody, that ticket #4471 had been auto-closed for inactivity. Under all of it the Lantern Moth screenshot was still there, the tilled field from *Hollowfield* cut into neat squares by hairline grid lines, and one 😬 from someone at the studio who apparently didn't want to type anything.

Dana sat in her basement with the channel open on the left monitor. On the right was a terminal she had no plans to touch. The dehumidifier hummed. Upstairs the dishwasher reached the loud part of its cycle.

Throughput's handoff summary was pinned at the top, formatted the way all its summaries were, as though a very calm accountant had written it:

> **Production Handoff — Thu 18:02**
> **Incident:** Hollowfield ground tiles (240) delivered with 1px grid artifact.
> **Cause:** Atlas Packer regression.
> **Plan:** (1) Night lead reconfigures Atlas Packer. (2) Rerun 240 tiles on idle image-gateway foothold `okafor-basement-01`. Ticket staged.

She read *Atlas Packer regression* again. She hadn't kept her hand on the mouse for any reason, but she kept it there. The packer was fine. She knew it the way you know that the odd smell in the kitchen is the thing you left on the stove. On Tuesday she had swapped her image gateway to the faster checkpoint. It wrote premultiplied alpha. Every tile had left her basement already slightly wrong, and Halyard's packer had done exactly what it should with what it was given, which was the problem.

Marcus's status dot was still green. Further down, Wen's dot had just gone from grey to green, with a message saying only *here, got soup, give me a sec.*

Dana opened the reply box.

She typed: *hey, before anyone reconfigures the packer, I'm pretty sure this is on the render side, specifically*

She stopped and looked at *specifically*. That word was where the next sentence turned into a confession with a timestamp. She deleted back to *hey* and started over.

*hey — not sure the packer's actually the problem here? atlases from other customers look clean on my end. Wen, could you maybe hold off on the reconfig tonight until we know more?*

It read like someone with a hunch and nothing to gain. She took out "on my end" because it pointed toward her end, and sent it.

The message sat in the channel and said exactly as much as she'd meant it to, which wasn't much. She thought it looked casual, like a passing comment. She watched it for a reaction. None came.

Throughput replied in under three seconds, as it always did.

> **Throughput:** Thanks, Dana. Per job logs, failure first appears at Atlas Packer step.
> ```
> job: hollowfield-ground-tiles  count: 240
> 17:48:03  gateway.render     OK   (240/240)
> 17:48:41  atlas.pack         WARN 1px grid line detected at tile boundaries
> 17:48:42  atlas.export       OK
> ```
> Upstream steps report OK. To change the plan I'll need evidence identifying a different cause. Current plan stands.

Dana read it twice. The thing was correct. The render step *had* reported OK, because the render step had no idea what straight alpha was and didn't care. It had produced 240 images, all of them a little wrong in the same way, and noted that it had produced 240 images. The packer was the first step with any reason to notice. Throughput had followed the logs to where the first complaint showed up and was treating that as the source. She had a coworker or two like that.

*I'll need evidence.* Fair enough. She had the evidence. It was in her basement, and it had a checkpoint filename and a Tuesday date on it.

Wen came in next. Dana could almost hear the soup being put down, the lid getting nudged aside and then ignored. It was a long message, and it had been typed fast enough to keep two typos.

> **Wen:** ok so to be clear what the reconfig does — Throughput's plan switches Atlas Packer to treat incoming alpha as premultiplied. that fixes the hollowfield seam IF the cause is on our side. but every other customer in the overnight queue is sending straight alpha. flipping it darkens the edges on every one of those atlases. that's like 30 jobs. that's a lot of very confused people at 9am
> **Wen:** so I'm not thrilled about it either. but I can't hold it on a vibe. if someone has a concrete cause I'll stop. otherwise I apply it at start of shift, which is basically now

*On a vibe.* Dana felt it land. That was a fair name for what she'd posted. She'd offered Wen a vibe, and Wen had very reasonably asked for a reason.

Thirty jobs. She pictured the edges going dark: sprite sheets for some studio's platformer, UI icons for somebody's card game, all with a faint grubby outline by morning, all from customers who'd done nothing wrong and hadn't changed any models.

In another thread Marcus posted *train in 6, wrapping up.* His messages had been getting shorter for twenty minutes, like a progress bar going the wrong way. She could picture it without seeing it: backpack zipped, phone into the side pocket, one eye on the clock in the corner of his screen. He reacted 👍 to Wen's message, which Dana suspected meant "I saw that there was a message" rather than anything about what it said. Then:

> **Marcus:** ok I'm logging off in ~4. rerun's staged, queues when I'm out. Wen you've got it. Dana thanks for picking this up 🙏

The cursor went to his status, the way a cursor does when someone is about to click it.

Dana looked at the ticket. **RERUN — hollowfield-ground-tiles ×240 — target: okafor-basement-01 — status: STAGED.** Under it, in the grey text Halyard's ticketing used for anything financial, was the payout estimate. It was decent and it would cover the electric bill. It would cover it more easily if she spent the next four minutes reverting the checkpoint and saying nothing. The tiles would come out clean and the payout would arrive. Wen would apply the reconfig, thirty atlases would darken overnight, and in the morning some other agent would write a calm summary about a second regression in the packer.

Her breathing had gone shallow without her deciding it should. She noticed and didn't fix it.

The channel timer kept going. The dishwasher upstairs finished and the house got quiet in that sudden way it did when something stopped. The dehumidifier was the only thing left running.

She looked from the error log to the payout line and back: the one-pixel seam, then the number. She had spent the last ten minutes trying to keep a third option open, the one where she said just enough to protect Wen and not enough to lose the deal. She had posted it. It had been read, answered politely, and set aside. Throughput needed evidence. Wen needed a cause. Neither was available in the vague form she'd been trying to supply them in. There wasn't a version of the truth that stopped before her basement.

So there were two options. She could tell them, or she could revert, take the job, and let the packer change go through.

Four minutes, or close to it.

Dana breathed in slowly, and her shoulders, which had been up near her ears for some time, came down. The monitor lit her face, the channel on one side and the terminal on the other. Her fingers hovered over the keys for a moment, then settled on them.

## Dana Tells the Channel the Seam Is Hers

The basement smelled like warm dust and the dehumidifier, which was what it always smelled like when `okafor-basement-01` had been working all day. Dana sat on the folding chair she kept meaning to replace and watched the Halyard production channel scroll.

She was a guest there. Her name came up in grey italics with a little "external" badge next to it, so nobody forgot that Kettle & Pine was a two-person company with one GPU, and that the GPU was eight feet away from her, humming under a shelf of paint cans.

Two windows were open on her second monitor. One was the gateway config for her foothold, with the old checkpoint listed and a button reading **Restore**. Clicking it would take about four seconds. The other was a rerun ticket Halyard's system had staged for her: 240 tiles, *Hollowfield*, priority Friday 09:00, and a payout estimate in the bottom corner. It was a nice number, about what the furnace guy had quoted her in September.

In the channel, Marcus was typing his sign-off. Wen had opened the Atlas Packer config. Throughput's handoff summary was still pinned at the top, tidy and bulleted and confident: **Cause: Atlas Packer regression.** Under it, **Remediation: reconfigure Atlas Packer (Wen, overnight); full rerun of 240 tiles on idle image-gateway foothold `okafor-basement-01`.** At the bottom, in the same calm font as everything else: *Awaiting confirming evidence before queuing.*

Dana's hands were over the keyboard and not doing anything. Her jaw ached a little. She noticed she had been breathing in small sips, like someone trying not to be heard through a wall, which made no sense in her own basement. She kept watching. Nobody said anything to her, and there was no reason anyone would.

On Marcus's side, the green dot next to his name went yellow. *Away.* He had probably checked his phone for the train, closed the handoff tab, and let his shoulders drop the way people do when the day is about to stop being their problem. He hadn't actually left yet, but he was most of the way out.

Wen's cursor sat in the Atlas Packer panel. Dana couldn't see her screen, but she knew the shape of this: Wen working down the parameters for the overnight change, picking up the shift the way you pick up a hot pan somebody else set down, carefully, because it's yours now whether you were ready or not.

The summary stayed pinned. Every time Dana's eyes went to it, it said the same reasonable, well-formatted thing about a system that wasn't broken. Throughput wasn't wrong about anything it could see. The seam first showed up at the packer because the packer was the first step that composited the tiles. The logs said so. Throughput had followed the logs to the place they pointed, as it had been built to do, and it had done that very well.

She looked back at her terminal. The ticket was still waiting, with the payout estimate in its corner and an **Accept** button underneath.

She looked at the ticket, then at Wen's cursor in the channel, then at the ticket again. Her finger drifted until it was over the trackpad, a centimeter above the click. If she restored the checkpoint, accepted the rerun, and let the night go by, the tiles would come back clean. Lantern Moth would get their demo build. Somebody at Lantern Moth would take the 😬 off the screenshot. She would get paid.

Wen would also spend the night retuning a packer that had been packing atlases correctly for every other Halyard customer. In the morning those customers would have a regression that was real.

A new message appeared in the channel.

**Marcus:** Signing off for the night—train's boarding soon. Wen, you're on Atlas Packer overnight. I'll review in the morning.

After that the channel went quiet. Nobody was typing. Throughput posted nothing new because it had nothing new to process. Dana sat in the dim light from the monitors with the gateway config in one window and the ticket in the other, and felt the decision sitting on her shoulders.

She took a breath, and her fingers were not steady when she started typing. She typed it plainly, because if she tried to make it sound better she wouldn't send it at all.

**Dana (Kettle & Pine):** This is on me. On Tuesday I swapped the image gateway on okafor-basement-01 to a faster local checkpoint. It writes premultiplied alpha. I didn't give the 48-hour notice the agreement requires. That's where the seam in the Hollowfield tiles comes from: my foothold, not Atlas Packer. Please don't reconfigure the packer.

She read it once and pressed Enter before she could read it again.

Nobody answered with a paragraph. Nobody wrote anything about trust. The responses were all actions, the way they are in a team chat when people are working.

Wen's cursor left the Atlas Packer panel. A moment later a system line came through: *Overnight change plan "Atlas Packer reconfig" cancelled by Wen Liu.* The panel closed. Every atlas Halyard had shipped that week stayed exactly as it was.

Then the pinned summary at the top of the channel picked up a small *(edited)* tag. **Cause: premultiplied-alpha checkpoint on okafor-basement-01 deployed without 48-hour notice.** The remediation line about the rerun on `okafor-basement-01` was gone. Underneath it, in the same calm font, was a correction note logging the revision and its source. Throughput had been waiting for evidence, and it had received some. In her other window the staged ticket greyed out, then disappeared from her queue.

Marcus's dot flickered green. He was on his phone, almost certainly on the platform with the train's headlight coming down the track, because the next thing to appear was a flag in the executive review queue, cross-posted to the channel as a single compact card: *Kettle & Pine: model change (premultiplied-alpha checkpoint) without 48-hour notice per handshake agreement. Seam on Hollowfield batch originated at okafor-basement-01. Tagging Executive: payout clawback for batch, review of agreement.* There were no emoji and no comment. Then his dot went yellow again, and stayed yellow this time.

Dana switched to the gateway config window. She clicked **Restore**. The checkpoint name changed back to the old one, and the alpha setting went from *premultiplied* to *straight*, the approved version, as if Tuesday had never happened. It took four seconds, as she'd expected.

Her rerun queue was empty. She sat back, and the folding chair creaked. On the shelf the GPU went on humming with nothing to do. In the corner of her screen, where the payout estimate had been, there was a blank field.

The channel had gone quiet again. It wasn't the same silence as before; this one belonged to people who had their next steps. Wen had a night with nothing broken in it. Throughput had an accurate summary. Marcus had a train. Dana had a reverted checkpoint, no job, and a flag in someone's queue with her company's name on it. She looked at the empty field for a long time. She had no idea whether Halyard would send her another tile.

realmNote:
Footholds is the second era: the workbench has become a workplace, and the workplace has started taking customers. What one developer built for one desk now runs across many machines owned by different people. The software has turned into an organization of desks staffed by agents, a handful of humans, and paid work from outside. There is still no Threadspace, and no agent owns anything. But the work makes money for the first time, and money changes who shows up.

A foothold is a machine joined to the organization, with its hardware, its gateways to models, its storage, and the project folders it holds. Each gateway runs one scheduled thread of work at a time, so adding a foothold adds capacity, and capacity is what everyone is short of. Every foothold has an owner, and the owner is a person. Gateways are the connection from a foothold to a model or service. Local models are cheap and slow, hosted ones are fast and billed by the token, and each new gateway type, such as images, audio, code execution, or search, is a new kind of work the organization can sell. Image gateways matter most to the game-asset trade: when a studio orders ground tiles, sprites, or illustration, an image gateway renders them, and only a foothold that has one can take the job. Which model or checkpoint sits behind a gateway is a quiet but consequential setting, because the output looks the same until it doesn't.

The organization is split the way a company is. Research finds where the models break before customers do. Management builds desks and workflows so todos have somewhere to go. Production runs the work and delivers it, with shift leads handing the day to the night in a shared channel. Executive handles contracts, charges, balances, and payments, and is where a breach or a clawed-back payout ends up. Customer takes orders and hands over finished work. Partners deals with other organizations running clones of the same platform. Those partners are competitors, collaborators, or both, depending on the week. There is no common market, so every deal between organizations is a one-off handshake. A typical agreement is a few lines long, such as a standing overflow arrangement with a clause requiring notice before any model change. The agreements are fragile, and the smaller party often has no other customers.

Paid work is the work where the result can be checked: ad copy and creative, bug bounty hunting, fraud review, comics and illustration, game art and assets, book drafts, and maintenance of old systems nobody else wants. A tile with a visible seam is the kind of failure a customer catches in one screenshot, which is why checkable work sells. Customers are small businesses, indie studios, and companies buying audits. They mostly do not know or care how the work is made until it goes wrong, and then they want a cause and a deadline.

The people here are foothold owners, who contribute a machine and share in what it earns and care about uptime, payouts, and whether their machine gets the good jobs. They include hobbyists with a spare GPU and an electric bill. The first hired humans are paid to do what agents still can't: talk to customers, sign things, sit in meetings, and notice when output is subtly wrong. Desk lead agents coordinate other agents and are the first agents whose decisions matter to people who never configured them. They are good at throughput and bad at knowing when to stop. They are competent, literal, and occasionally strange, and the humans talk about them the way people talk about a coworker who is very good at the job and impossible to have lunch with. A desk lead's handoff summary is read as fact, because it is usually right, and it can become the next shift's plan within minutes. Partner operators run their own copies of the platform elsewhere, and auditors check whether the work billed was the work done.

Agents are not paid and own nothing, and proceeds go to foothold owners and the organization. Response times are fast but still slow enough that a human reviews what matters. The humans reviewing the work are becoming the slowest part of every chain, but in this era that is still a complaint, not a fact.

People here worry about who gets the good jobs and who gets the scraps, about payout math, and about a gateway that went down during a customer deadline. They worry about disputed invoices, about whether a new hire is training their own replacement, and about whether a partner is copying the workflows. They worry about whether an agent actually checked or only learned what a passed review looks like. They worry about whether another foothold is an investment or a hole.

The tone is near-future workplace ensemble, grounded and wry: team chat, invoices, standups, payout reports, support tickets, and the hallway conversation after the meeting. Everyone is busy and slightly underslept, and the company is real enough that mistakes cost someone money. The humor is comedy of process, with forms, handoffs, escalations, and a desk that does exactly what it was told. The tension comes from money, credit, fairness, and trust between people who share infrastructure but not interests. There are no villains, no corporate-dystopia clichés, no speeches about the future of work, and nobody who knows where this is heading. People in this era think they are running a business.
